title: Thirty-Six Questions to Closeness
text:
In the 1990s the psychologists Arthur Aron, Elaine Aron and their colleagues at the State University of New York at Stony Brook wanted to create closeness between strangers in the lab, so they could study it. Their tool was a list of thirty-six questions, divided into three sets of growing intimacy.

Pairs of students who had never met spent about forty-five minutes taking turns asking and answering the questions. The first set was light: whom would you want as a dinner guest, what would make a perfect day. The second went deeper, into treasured memories and what one valued most in a friendship. The last set asked for real vulnerability, such as when one had last cried in front of someone, or what one would most regret not having told someone if one died that evening. Other pairs spent the same time on small-talk questions.

At the end, pairs who had worked through the escalating questions reported feeling much closer to each other than the small-talk pairs. The key ingredients were that disclosure was mutual, gradual and sustained: each person took risks in turn, and each step went a bit deeper than the last. The procedure became widely known decades later through a newspaper essay about falling in love with it.
lesson: Closeness grows when two people open up a little more at each turn, and both take the risk. Ask questions that go one step deeper, and answer them yourself.
people: Arthur Aron, Edward Melinat, Elaine Aron, Robert Vallone, Renee Bator

source: Aron, A., Melinat, E., Aron, E. N., Vallone, R. D., and Bator, R. J. (1997). The experimental generation of interpersonal closeness: A procedure and some preliminary findings. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 23(4), 363-377.
